lesson.title: Tour of the 7 Strong Verb Classes
lesson.subtitle: Walk every ablaut class with two exemplar verbs — recognize class by vowel melody

hook.title: The Hall of Fame
hook.content: Proto-Germanic sorted its strong verbs into seven classes by vowel melody — and the numbering is still on the wall in every German grammar. You have met members of every class already; this tour hangs them in order. Class I: ei–ei–ie? German'sreiben-family — schreiben, schrieb. Class II: ziehen, zog. Class III: singen, sang, gesungen and finden, fand. Class IV: sprechen, sprach — the -n- verbs. Class V: geben, gab. Class VI: fahren, fuhr. Class VII: schlafen, schlief — the old reduplicating class that survives as a simple vowel change. Two exemplars each, and the hall is yours.

footnotes.title: Class VII's Secret
footnotes.content: The seventh class was once the REDUPLICATING class — ancients said *lelōb 'they let'. German smoothed it to a vowel change (schlafen, schlief; fallen, fiel) with no consonant doubling. Gothic, the fossil language, still shows the reduplication: fai-falh 'hid'. The hall's oldest room.

pattern.title: The Seven Rooms
pattern.content: Room I (ei–ei–ie): schreiben, schrieb, geschrieben ↔ describe, described — the scribe family. Room II (ie–o–o): ziehen, zog, gezogen — the tow family. Room III (i–a–u): singen, sang, gesungen; trinken, trank; finden, fand, gefunden — the biggest room, with English sing/drink/find beside them. Room IV (e–a–o): sprechen, sprach, gesprochen; kommen? no — kommen is its own oddity (kam, gekommen); stehlen (steal — stahl!). Room V (e–a–e): geben, gab, gegeben; nehmen, nahm, genommen — the give/take room. Room VI (a–u–a): fahren, fuhr, gefahren — the fare family. Room VII (ä/au–ie): schlafen, schlief; fallen, fiel — the reduplicating relics. Walk it twice and the melodies stick.
pattern.linguist_note: The classes are defined by the PIE root syllable's structure (e/o ablaut + following consonant), which is why verbs that look unrelated share melodies: Germanic inherited the room assignments wholesale, and both languages redecorated independently.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb to its class melody:
exercises.target_answer: schrieb / geschrieben, zog / gezogen, sprach / gesprochen, schlief / geschlafen
exercises.explanation: ei–ie, ie–o–o, e–a–o, and the reduplicating relic — four of the seven rooms on one wall.

exercises.prompt: A NEW verb: 'werfen' (to throw) goes 'warf, geworfen'. Which room does it live in?
options: Room IV — the e–a–o room, with sprechen, sprach, gesprochen
No room — it is a weak verb
Room III — the i–a–u room, with singen and trinken
exercises.target_answer: Room IV — the e–a–o room, with sprechen, sprach, gesprochen
exercises.explanation: werfen, warf, geworfen — hear the melody and you know the room, even for verbs you have never studied. That is the hall's power.

exercises.prompt: Which room holds the REDUPLICATING relic (once *le-lōb-style forms)?
options: Room VII — schlafen, schlief; fallen, fiel
exercises.target_answer: Room VII — schlafen, schlief; fallen, fiel
exercises.meaning: The oldest room in the hall
exercises.explanation: Class VII reduplicated its past in the ancient language; German smoothed it to a vowel change, Gothic kept the doubling.

exercises.prompt: Which English verb shares Room VI's melody with 'fahren, fuhr'?
exercises.explanation: Same class, same root, same a–u slide — English and German filed it in the same room 2,000 years ago.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the German sentence for 'We drank water and sang':
exercises.target_answer: Wir haben Wasser getrunken und gesungen

vocab_hints.note: Room III: i–a–u — trinken, trank, getrunken

exercises.explanation: Two Room III participles (getrunken, gesungen) chained behind one haben — the hall of fame, live.

summary.outcome: Place any strong verb in its class by vowel melody and predict its forms.

use_example.german: Wir haben Wasser getrunken und gesungen.

summary.takeaway: Seven rooms, two exemplars each — hear the melody, know the class, predict the paradigm.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Motion → Accusative, Location → Dative — the two-way preposition drill isle.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — build in German: "We sing here today"
twist.explanation: Building "Wir singen heute hier" from the lesson's core pattern locks in Tour of the 7 Strong Verb Classes.

singen.etymology_derivation: Initial S voiced to [z] before vowels.

trinken.context_translation: I drink a glass of water.

finden.context_translation: I cannot find it / I find it not.
finden.etymology_derivation: Stem find + infinitive -en (German keeps pure short [ɪ] vowel).

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

schlafen.etymology_derivation: p → f with sl- → schl- cluster.

ziehen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
ziehen.etymology_derivation: t → z [ts] (Proto-Germanic *teuhaną, cognate with English tow / tug).

schreiben.etymology_derivation: A Latin loan (scribere) that both languages Germanicized — English kept it in scribe, script, describe. Strong verb: schrieb, geschrieben. [wiktionary]

scheinen.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *skīnan — class 1 strong verb (schien, geschienen), ablaut-matching shine/shone. [wiktionary]

viel.context_translation: We are having a lot of fun.
viel.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *felu 'many', from PIE *pleh₁- — English once had the twin word fele 'many', the very entry Wiktionary points to. [wiktionary]

muskel.etymology_derivation: A learned borrowing around 1700 from Latin musculus, the same Latin word that gave English muscle. [wiktionary]

pille.context_phrase: Die Pille liegt auf dem Tisch.
pille.context_translation: The pill is lying on the table.
pille.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German pille, from Latin pilula (little ball) — the same Latin word behind English pill. [wiktionary]

automat.context_phrase: Am Automat kaufe ich ein Ticket.
automat.context_translation: At the machine I buy a ticket.
automat.etymology_derivation: A learned borrowing from Latin automatum, from Greek automatos, self-acting — the same Greek word behind English automatic; American English automat came from German. [wiktionary]

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: English and German share the 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels rather than adding endings.
strong_verbs_ablaut.philological_note: Joseph Wright's Historical German Grammar categorizes these 7 classes. Knowing "sing-sang-sung" gives you "singen-sang-gesungen", "drink-drank-drunk" gives you "trinken-trank-getrunken", and "drive-drove-driven" gives you "treiben-trieb-getrieben".
